extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing patent claims for subject-matter eligibility under the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (IEG), using business-method examples. Applies the two-step (Step 1 / Step 2A / Step 2B) framework and related case-law considerations to determine whether claims are patent eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category determination (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a device or set of devices (e.g., a system, machine), it is a machine and thus satisfies Step 1 (Step 1: YES). Being in a statutory category does not end the analysis — proceed to Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the focus of the claim is on a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon) — i.e., whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claim concept to categories/case law (e.g., abstract ideas like organizing human behavior, data collection/recognition/storage, intermediated settlement, risk hedging). If claim is similar to prior abstract-idea holdings, conclude Step 2A: Yes and proceed to Step 2B unless claim is readily seen as an improvement in computer-related technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Enfish improvement-in-computer-technology exception at Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the claim is 'directed to' a specific improvement in computer-related technology (as in Enfish), in which case it may not be an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is clearly directed to an improvement in how computers operate or to computer functionality itself, the analysis can end at Step 2A with eligibility. If not readily apparent, proceed to Step 2B. Examples: Enfish claims were non-abstract because they improved computer functionality; BASCOM involved a close call where internet-centric/technology-improvement reasoning could end analysis at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept/inventive-concept inquiry (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether any element or combination of elements in the claim is sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (i.e., provides an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both individual limitations and the ordered combination. An inventive concept can arise from an unconventional, non-generic combination of known elements that yields a technology-based solution or improvement. If the additional elements, viewed individually or as an ordered combination, are insufficient, Step 2B: No (ineligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether additional limitations are merely generic computer/network components
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether recited computer/network components are generic and perform generic functions at a high level of generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic recitations (e.g., local client computer, Internet computer network, remote server, processor, memory) that perform conventional functions do not amount to significantly more when taken individually. Such limitations, described at a high level, normally fail to supply an inventive concept unless combined in an unconventional, non-routine way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claim limitations reflect activity that was well-known, routine, or conventional at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification and, where appropriate, external evidence to evaluate conventionality. If limitations are well-understood, routine, and conventional, they do not contribute to a finding of 'significantly more.' The guidance notes examiners should consider whether the combination is 'not well-understood, routine or conventional.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether the combination yields a technology-based solution or an improvement in the technological field
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the ordered combination of claim elements provides a technical improvement or solves a technological problem in a particular technical environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim's combination offers benefits or improvements over prior art technical systems (e.g., improvement in Internet content filtering, 3-D coordinate reconstruction from overlapping camera views), and is not merely an abstract-idea-based solution implemented with generic components, then the combination can amount to significantly more (eligible). BASCOM and certain inventory-camera-array examples illustrate technology-based solutions that confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the abstract idea by mapping claim language to prior court-identified abstract concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting, explicitly identify the abstract idea reflected in the claim by pointing to claim language and analogizing to concepts courts have deemed abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection should state which claim language describes the abstract idea (e.g., fraud prevention by identity verification; inventory management; filtering content) and explain why that concept is similar to prior cases (CyberSource, Content Extraction, Digitech, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize pre-solution activity and mere data gathering as insignificant
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat steps that are mere data gathering or pre-solution activity as insufficient to confer an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps like 'obtaining customer-specific information' performed at a high level of generality are often pre-solution activity and insignificant to Step 2B. Such steps are typically considered conventional actions necessary to use the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic automation of a business practice is not significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Automating an economic or business practice on generic computers does not, by itself, make a claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim merely automates what bank tellers or other human actors did previously, or generically implements price optimization or verification on computers, it typically fails Step 2B (examples: OIP, Intellectual Ventures I, Accenture, Ultramercial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and plain meaning in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims under examination are given their broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification; claim terms default to plain meaning absent special definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply BRI when analyzing the claim scope and the abstract-idea inquiry; the examples explicitly assume BRI when examining recently filed applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the specification and factual record to assess conventionality or inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the specification's descriptions of technical problems/solutions and any record evidence when determining whether limitations are conventional or reflect inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification can show that a claimed combination was not well-understood or routine and can support a finding that the claim provides a technological improvement. Examiners may add remarks or reasons for allowance if the record would benefit from clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a claim is a 'close call', consider internet-centrism or clear technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is a close call whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, determine whether the claim is internet-centric or clearly directed to an improvement in computer technology; if so, find not directed to abstract idea (end at Step 2A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BASCOM claim was described as a 'close call.' If an examiner skilled in the art recognizes the claim as internet-centric or as an improvement in the technology of filtering, it would be appropriate to find the claim not directed to the abstract idea and finish the analysis at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting a proper rejection: explain why additional limitations amount only to generic computer functions
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection, explain clearly why the additional limitations are insufficient (e.g., mere generic computer components, conventional activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should identify the abstract idea, point to claim language describing it, and explain why the additional claim limitations amount to no more than generic computer functions or conventional activity in the particular technological environment (cite case analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action/allowance remarks when claim is eligible but recites an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites an abstract idea but is nonetheless eligible because of inventive concept, examiners may add remarks to the Office action or reasons for allowance indicating both points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners can document that the claim recites the abstract idea yet explain why, after Step 2B analysis of the ordered combination (e.g., technology-based solution, unconventional combination), the claim is eligible; such remarks can help the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting selection/manipulation of particular information remain abstract absent technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely selecting, recognizing, storing or manipulating particular information (e.g., image sequences, classification/location data) does not make the concept any less abstract without a meaningful technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric Power Group, Digitech, Content Extraction indicate that information manipulation alone is abstract. To be eligible, the claim must integrate the abstract idea into a specific practical application that improves technology (e.g., 3-D reconstruction from overlapping camera views).

rubrics_metrics.name: System/machine claim status alone does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a system claim may be a 'machine' (statutory category), that status alone does not resolve the abstract-idea inquiry or confer eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if Step 1 is satisfied (machine), the claim must still be analyzed under Step 2A/2B. Generic machine recitations (memory, processor) performing routine functions typically do not make the claim significantly more.
